description: Width tiers for Year 1 Science — ACARA v9. Covers the three U-strand descriptors. H-strand and I-strand (1–2 band) are in science_y1_2_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor — fewest phenomena or contexts that still genuinely satisfy the descriptor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding phenomena, cultural contexts or applications. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data. Typical grounded in common cases.

AC9S1U01.minimum_width: Name the four basic needs (air, water, food, shelter) and give one example of each being met for a named living thing; identify one habitat and describe how two features meet the needs of a living thing found there.
AC9S1U01.typical_width: Identify and compare needs of a variety of plants and animals including humans; describe how multiple habitats meet living thing needs; connect students' own caring experiences to need-meeting; explain why removing a living thing from its habitat threatens its survival.
wider: Recognise how First Nations Australians care for living things — examining traditional ecological knowledge of plant and animal needs on Country
Learn from local ecologists or wildlife carers about observing animal behaviour to design habitat supports (frog hotels, nesting boxes)
Explore why caring for plants and animals matters as sources of food, fibre and ecological balance
elaborations: identifying the places where plants and animals live including homes, local ponds, parks, gardens or zoos
identifying what they do to look after pets or plants at home and grouping these activities
identifying and comparing the needs of a variety of plants and animals including humans
creating dioramas of a place a plant or animal lives identifying features that enable need-meeting
recognising how First Nations Australians care for living things
exploring why caring for plants and animals is important including as sources of food and fibre

AC9S1U02.minimum_width: Describe at least two observable daily changes and at least two seasonal differences; describe one way daily change and one way seasonal change affect everyday life.
AC9S1U02.typical_width: Make and record observations of daily weather and seasonal plant patterns; identify seasonal patterns in plant behaviour (leaf change, flowering) and animal behaviour (hibernation, migration); explain how daily and seasonal patterns inform human clothing choices and activity planning.
wider: Recognise the extensive knowledges of daily and seasonal change held by First Nations Australians — examining traditional seasonal calendars beyond the European four-season framework
Explore how First Nations Australians' concepts of time and weather patterns explain how things happen in the world
Investigate how seasonal changes affect animals including hibernation and migration
elaborations: making and recording observations of weather, seasonal plant changes and growth of flowers or fruit
noticing how daily and seasonal patterns help us make plans for activities
investigating how seasonal changes affect plants and animals including hibernation and migration
exploring how people make clothing choices using weather predictions or seasonal knowledge
recognising First Nations Australians' extensive knowledges of daily and seasonal changes
exploring how First Nations Australians' concepts of time and weather patterns explain the world

AC9S1U03.minimum_width: Identify at least three everyday objects requiring push or pull; describe the direction and compare the strength of each force; describe how a push or pull affects the motion of one object and the shape of one object; make a prediction before observing.
AC9S1U03.typical_width: Observe and manipulate everyday objects identifying push/pull forces with direction and strength; predict and describe effects on motion (start, stop, direction change) and shape (squash, stretch); represent forces using labels, arrows or role-play.
wider: Investigate the push and pull movements of traditional First Nations Australians' children's instructive toys
Explore how traditional Asian toys (kendama, Daruma Otoshi, shuttlecock) are played using push or pull forces
Investigate how sporting equipment design produces stronger pushes and pulls — connecting force to design
Explore how engineers use force knowledge to create playground equipment or toys (AC9S1H01)
elaborations: observing and manipulating everyday objects such as playground equipment, toys, windows or doors
investigating how sporting equipment design produces stronger pushes and pulls
recognising that pushing or pulling can start, stop or change direction of motion
exploring how playdough shape changes when pushed or pulled
designing playground equipment or toys representing push and pull forces
investigating push and pull in traditional First Nations children's instructive toys
exploring how traditional Asian toys are played using push or pull
